design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (Hedges' g) of case-control PET and SPECT studies comparing striatal dopamine measures (stimulant-induced dopamine release, dopamine transporter [DAT] availability, D2/3 receptor availability; VMAT2, dopamine synthesis and D1 described without pooling) between people who use cocaine or amphetamine/methamphetamine and healthy controls. Whole striatum only. Databases: PubMed, EMBASE and PsycINFO from inception to 14 May 2016 (Abstract › Data sources); search strings, selection flow and inclusion details are in a supplement. Language limits, grey literature and hand-searching are not stated in the main text. No protocol or registration is mentioned.
can_establish: That published case-control imaging studies, taken together, report lower striatal DAT availability and lower D2/3 receptor availability in people who use amphetamine-type stimulants than in controls, with the DAT difference the largest, and lower stimulant-induced dopamine release mainly in cocaine users.
cannot_establish: Whether the differences were caused by stimulant use, preceded it, reflect loss of terminals or regulation, or change with abstinence (every primary study is cross-sectional and the review ran no analysis by abstinence duration, smoking or other drug use), nor how trustworthy the primary studies are (their risk of bias was not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Primary studies identified by database search; recruitment of their participants not summarized in the main text (study characteristics are in the supplement, not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: studies of the striatal dopamine system in cocaine or amphetamine/methamphetamine users with a control group, reporting means and SDs for both groups (Methods › Study selection). One cocaine DAT study was excluded because participants had HIV (Results › Dopamine transporter). Two cocaine DAT PET studies had overlapping samples (Results › Dopamine transporter). Duplicate screening and duplicate extraction are not described in the main text.
sample.demographics: Not summarized in the main text; extracted variables (age, sex, substance use, comorbid substance use, abstinence confirmation and duration, diagnosis, imaging method) are listed in Methods › Data extraction.
sample.selection_effects: Only studies reporting group means and SDs were eligible. The amphetamine-type group mixes methamphetamine-dependent people with recreational dexamphetamine users (two included studies by Schrantee and Schouw). The abstract states that in most studies abstinence lasted 5 days to 3 weeks, so pooled estimates largely describe early abstinence. Possible sample overlap among studies from the same groups (two DAT studies by Volkow and colleagues, two by McCann and colleagues) is not discussed.

exposure.measurement: As defined in each primary study; the review extracted diagnosis, method of abstinence confirmation and duration of abstinence but does not report them in the main text.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not summarized in the main text.
exposure.polysubstance: Comorbid substance use was extracted but not analysed. The Limitations note that studies varied in nicotine and alcohol use and abstinence, and assert that such variation would obscure rather than account for the effects (Discussion › Limitations); no analysis supports this.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Majority of studies: 5 days to 3 weeks (Abstract › Results). VMAT2 studies in methamphetamine users had mean abstinence of 2.6 days, 19 days and about 3 months (Results › Other dopaminergic measures). No analysis by abstinence duration.

comparison.controls: Healthy controls of the primary studies.
comparison.matching: Matching within primary studies not summarized or assessed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No primary study had a pre-use measure; the review discusses a model in which lower dopamine markers precede use but cannot test it (Discussion, models paragraphs).

outcomes.instruments: Whole-striatum PET/SPECT indices: change in D2/3 binding after an amphetamine or methylphenidate challenge (dopamine release); DAT availability; D2/3 receptor availability; also VMAT2 availability, [18F]-DOPA uptake and D1 availability. Effect size Hedges' g, users minus controls.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note D2/3 tracers do not separate D2 from D3 or high- from low-affinity states and are sensitive to endogenous dopamine; tracer interaction with methamphetamine may lower VMAT2 estimates in early abstinence (Discussion; Results › Other dopaminergic measures).
outcomes.operationalization: An alteration is a pooled standardized group difference with p<0.05.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; seven pooled analyses each at p<0.05 (two-tailed).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. No risk-of-bias tool was applied to the primary studies (none mentioned in Methods).

analysis.effect_sizes: All pooled estimates (Hedges' g, random effects, whole striatum; Results). Dopamine release: all stimulants, 7 studies, 164 users vs 139 controls, g=−0.84 (95% CI −1.08 to −0.60), p<0.001; cocaine only, 5 studies, g=−0.87 (−1.15 to −0.60), p<0.001; amphetamine-type, 2 studies, not pooled: SMD −1.05 (−1.76 to −0.34) and −0.40 (−1.11 to 0.32). DAT: all stimulants, 12 studies, 177 vs 191, g=−0.91 (−1.50 to −0.32), p<0.01; amphetamine-type, 9 studies, 108 vs 126, g=−1.47 (−1.83 to −1.10), p<0.001; cocaine not pooled (two SPECT studies in acute abstinence found higher DAT, two overlapping PET studies no difference). D2/3 receptors: all stimulants, 19 studies, 342 vs 321, g=−0.76 (−0.92 to −0.60), p<0.001; cocaine, 12 studies, g=−0.73 (−0.94 to −0.53), p<0.001; amphetamine-type, 7 studies, g=−0.81 (−1.12 to −0.49), p<0.001. Not pooled: [18F]-DOPA in cocaine users (1 study) 0.46 (−0.46 to 1.39); VMAT2 (4 studies) lower in cocaine users at 2 weeks, g 1.6 (0.68 to 2.52), and in methamphetamine users at 3 months, g 1.68 (0.86 to 2.5), but higher in two methamphetamine studies in early abstinence, g 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76); D1 (1 cocaine study) no difference. Heterogeneity: described as low except for DAT; I², τ² and prediction intervals are not given in the main text (supplement). Forest plots (Figures 1–3) are images and were not extracted.
analysis.covariates: None. The only moderator analysis is the split by drug class (study-level). No meta-regression on abstinence duration, smoking, alcohol, tracer or route; leave-one-out sensitivity analyses reported only in the supplement.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned in the main text.
analysis.selective_reporting: Publication bias assessed by funnel plots and regression tests, with results only in the supplement; the main text says only that the funnel plots show few large studies (Discussion › Limitations). No adjusted estimate. Sensitivity and heterogeneity results are also confined to the supplement.
analysis.power: Not reported. The amphetamine-type release question rests on 2 small studies; FDOPA, D1 and VMAT2 on 1–4 studies each.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooled case-control differences: lower striatal DAT (g −1.47 in amphetamine-type users, mostly early abstinence), lower D2/3 availability (g −0.81 amphetamine-type, −0.73 cocaine) and lower stimulant-induced release (pooled mainly from cocaine studies). VMAT2 findings in methamphetamine users go in both directions depending on abstinence. Primary studies were not appraised for risk of bias and no confounder or abstinence analysis was run.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that pre- and post-synaptic dopamine function is down-regulated in stimulant users, and the Conclusions call the evidence robust with large effect sizes and recommend restoring dopamine function as a treatment target (Abstract › Conclusion; Conclusions). Down-regulation names a mechanism the cross-sectional data cannot identify; the Discussion itself sets out adaptive, pre-existing and hybrid models and states the findings do not address the temporal relationship (Discussion, models paragraphs). The release finding is generalized to all stimulants though only two amphetamine-type studies exist. The Discussion calls g of −0.76 to −0.91 large to very large. Robustness is asserted without any risk-of-bias assessment, and the claim that confounding by nicotine or alcohol could only obscure the effects is not tested.

timeline.event: Earliest included amphetamine-type DAT study: 6 abstinent methamphetamine users and 4 methcathinone users vs 10 controls (McCann et al., 1998; appraised in this batch).
Critical assessment of whether dopamine-marker reductions in methamphetamine users mean neuronal damage

replication.where_it_stands: The authors describe this as the first meta-analysis of these imaging findings (Discussion, 1st paragraph). The DAT reduction in amphetamine-type users is the most consistent pooled finding; its meaning (terminal loss, regulation or pre-existing difference) and its course with abstinence are not addressed by the pooled data.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered update with risk-of-bias appraisal of each imaging study, individual-participant or meta-regression analysis of DAT by abstinence duration, tobacco and other drug use, and separate pooling of VMAT2 by abstinence phase; ultimately, prospective imaging before and after the onset of regular use.

Random-effects Hedges' g, but unadjusted group means from non-randomized studies were pooled without justification, and the combined DAT estimate pools cocaine studies whose effects run in the opposite direction (higher DAT) with amphetamine-type studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: More than one critical flaw: no protocol, no risk-of-bias assessment of the primary studies and no account of it in the interpretation, pooling of unadjusted observational data (including opposite-direction cocaine DAT results in the combined estimate), and publication-bias results not discussed. Items 4, 5, 7 and 8 were judged from the main text only, because the supplement is a downloadable .docx that was not opened; the overall rating does not depend on them. Critically low confidence describes the review's methods, not the direction of the DAT finding, which is consistent across the amphetamine-type studies.

key_findings.finding: DAT availability in amphetamine-type stimulant users (9 studies, 108 users vs 126 controls): g=−1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10), p<0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dopamine transporter, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results

key_findings.finding: DAT availability, all stimulants (12 studies: 3 cocaine, 9 amphetamine-type; 177 users vs 191 controls): g=−0.91 (−1.50 to −0.32), p<0.01. Cocaine studies were inconsistent: two SPECT studies in acute abstinence (up to 4 days; mean 7 days) found higher DAT, two overlapping PET studies found no difference; one study excluded for HIV comorbidity.

D2/3 receptor availability: all stimulants, 19 studies, 342 users vs 321 controls, g=−0.76 (−0.92 to −0.60); cocaine, 12 studies, g=−0.73 (−0.94 to −0.53); amphetamine-type, 7 studies, g=−0.81 (−1.12 to −0.49); all p<0.001.

Stimulant-induced dopamine release: all stimulants, 7 studies, 164 users vs 139 controls, g=−0.84 (−1.08 to −0.60); cocaine only, 5 studies, g=−0.87 (−1.15 to −0.60); amphetamine-type users only 2 studies, not pooled, SMD −1.05 (−1.76 to −0.34) and −0.40 (−1.11 to 0.32).

VMAT2 (not pooled, 4 studies): lower in cocaine users at 2 weeks' abstinence (g 1.6, 0.68 to 2.52) and in methamphetamine users after 3 months (g 1.68, 0.86 to 2.5); higher in two studies of methamphetamine users in early abstinence (mean 2.6 and 19 days; g 1.16, 0.56 to 1.76). The authors note tracer binding may be underestimated in early abstinence because methamphetamine acts at the same VMAT2 site.
key_findings.note: Signs as printed: reductions and increases are both given as positive g; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Dopamine synthesis ([18F]-DOPA): one cocaine study, described as showing reduced synthesis capacity, effect size 0.46 (−0.46 to 1.39); no amphetamine-type study. D1 receptors: one cocaine study, no group difference.
In most included studies abstinence lasted 5 days to 3 weeks.
Heterogeneity was described as low in all analyses except DAT; no I², τ² or prediction interval is printed in the main text. Funnel plots showed few large studies; test results are in the supplement.

The authors set out three models (adaptive down-regulation, pre-existing reductions, hybrid) and state that the data cannot address the temporal relation between dopamine changes and phase of addiction; they cite human DAT recovery with abstinence and the one post-mortem study (reduced DAT without neuron loss) against neuron loss, and two registry studies of Parkinson's disease risk in its favour.

The 31 studies and 519 users vs 512 controls in the abstract equal the D2/3 set (19 studies, 342/321) plus the DAT set (12 studies, 177/191); the release studies are a subset of the D2/3 set, and the VMAT2, DOPA and D1 studies are outside the count (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend presents g=−0.91 (−1.50 to −0.32) as the decrease in methamphetamine users, but the Results give −0.91 as the all-stimulant DAT estimate (including cocaine) and −1.47 as the amphetamine-type estimate.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Figure 2 legend; Results › Dopamine transporter)
reporting_issues.consequence: Anyone citing the figure would understate the amphetamine-type DAT difference and misattribute the combined estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 4 legend lists pooled estimates of −0.81 (−1.34 to −0.29) and −0.71 (−0.91 to −0.52) that match no estimate in the Results (release −0.84 [−1.08 to −0.60]; D2/3 −0.76 [−0.92 to −0.60]; D2/3 amphetamine-type −0.81 [−1.12 to −0.49]).
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly left over from an earlier analysis; only the Results values should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Effect-size signs are inconsistent: reductions in DAT, D2/3 and release are negative, but VMAT2 reductions are given as positive g (1.6, 1.68), VMAT2 increases also as positive (1.16), and a DOPA effect described as reduced is positive (0.46) with an interval that includes zero.
reporting_issues.consequence: Direction must be taken from the words, and the DOPA finding is not statistically significant despite being described as a reduction.

reporting_issues.issue: A single g (1.16, 0.56 to 1.76) is given for two VMAT2 studies after the review says too few studies existed to pool such measures.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooling method for this figure is not described.

reporting_issues.issue: The two cocaine PET studies showing no DAT difference are cited as refs 26 and 37 in the Results but as 26 and 54 in the Discussion (ref 54 is a DAT occupancy study).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Dopamine transporter; Discussion, 1st paragraph)

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes g of −0.84, −0.91 and −0.76 as large to very large effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: By conventional benchmarks these are medium-to-large; the wording overstates magnitude.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's 31 studies are described as measuring synthesis or release, DAT or receptors, but the count and participant totals match only the D2/3 and DAT sets.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the synthesis, VMAT2 and D1 studies were described but not counted or pooled.
